subject: Humanities
objective_verbatim: Study the Holocaust sensitively (Holocaust Memorial Day).
focus: Lives before persecution, removal of rights, actions and responsibility

source_workbook.basis: Owner brief plus accepted Week 1 next_lesson_reference_only record. Workbook not re-read for this return.

source_cells.basis: Owner brief; next-outcome record in accepted Week 1

assessment_generic: Formative historical understanding only. No award completion inferred.
sensitive_response_route: Point to PAUSE or tell the adult quietly. Use the agreed supervised place. You do not need to explain to the group. When ready, choose a private recap or the quiet task. The adult will help you rejoin.
quiet_alternative: Quiet task: put these times in order: 14:00 club; 08:30 library; 12:00 lunch; 10:00 break. Copy or point to the first and last. Add a clock face if you wish. These are made-up daily times. You do not need to use the history cards.
staff_care_rules: Before teaching, review the school’s chosen memorial-day resource with the designated lead. Use it as a staff reference and check it against these care rules. No extra footage, camp photographs, testimony, graphic imagery or unplanned live browsing is used in this lesson.

Preview the content privately where helpful. Do not ask pupils to imagine being victims, take historical roles, defend prejudice, rank suffering or disclose family history. Never appoint a Jewish pupil as a spokesperson. The sources are original factual summaries, not testimony or archive extracts.

Agree a discreet PAUSE signal, named responsible adult within the school’s usual arrangements, supervised quiet place and return check before starting. If supervision away from the room is unavailable, offer a calm space in the room and seek normal support. If the sole adult cannot supervise both learners, pause the whole group. Do not send a pupil away alone.

For distress, stop the demand, acknowledge it calmly and offer the agreed route without a public explanation or sanction. Do not probe or insist on a historical recap while the pupil is upset. Listen to disclosures and follow the school’s existing safeguarding arrangements; record only what is needed in the appropriate private system.

For an antisemitic remark, interrupt calmly and firmly. Name the harm without repeating a slur. Explain that hostility towards Jewish people is antisemitism and is unacceptable. Jewish people were not responsible for their persecution. Correct the falsehood with a brief fact; do not debate Holocaust denial or ask pupils to defend Jewish people’s rights.

For flippancy or laughter, stop and reset the expectation of respect. A nervous response is possible, but harm still needs addressing. Follow up privately, check those affected and use existing behaviour and safeguarding procedures for targeted, repeated or serious incidents. Avoid public shaming or speculative labels about the pupil.

Offer the neutral quiet task and a private check on readiness to return. The alternative is not evidence of the Holocaust outcome. Record the history work as deferred or not yet evidenced, with a later supported offer. There is no penalty for taking the agreed pause.
definition: The Holocaust was the planned persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany, its allies and those who helped them. It took place from 1933 to 1945. The Nazis also persecuted and murdered millions of other people. Their experiences were not all the same.
historical_name_rule: Real historical names, places and dates allowed by owner; no living private identities.
source_card_status: Teacher-written factual summaries, not testimony or original historical extracts.

model: S2 dates the state-job law to 7 April 1933 in Germany. It began removing Jewish people from state work, though early exceptions existed. Losing work could remove income. Officials who enforced the rule helped persecution happen. Jewish people were not to blame.
success_criteria: Identify one aspect of Jewish life before persecution.
Explain effects of two dated restrictions with place and source codes.
Explain actions or inaction of perpetrators, bystanders and rescuers.
Reflect on remembrance and responsibility today.

hinge.question: Which explains a change to rights? A: 1938 came after 1935. B: The school ban cut access to education and separated pupils from classmates. C: Every country used the same rules on the same date.
hinge.answer_and_decision_rule: B. A orders dates but gives no effect. C is false: place and date matter. Check both learners privately. If either needs help, model S2 as date + change + effect, then use the parallel check before independent work.
hinge.parallel: Parallel check: What did the 1935 laws and later rules take away from German Jews? Answer: citizenship and political rights. Ask the learner to identify Germany and explain that law does not mean fairness.

pair_work: Evidence Finder locates an action and source; Explainer states an effect; swap. These are learning roles, never historical roles. Each pupil produces an individual record.

evidence.common_finish: Keep your own record: one fact about Jewish life before persecution; two dated changes to rights with source codes and an effect; one action or inaction for each of the three roles; and one thought on remembrance and care today.

communication: Offer to the Communication portfolio. Record R only after the learner gives an idea, an adult audience replies with one NS (next step), and the learner responds in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. Record E only after actual banking. Keep the response mode and help used. A partner answer does not establish both learners’ understanding.
memorial_day: 27 January annually; distinct from this lesson on 12 January.

next_requested_return_reference_only.outcome_verbatim: Use sources to investigate a campaign for rights and change.

Lives, rights and choices: cards
Tuesday 12 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 2 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W02
White paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
These are teacher-written factual summaries. They are not archive extracts or testimony. No real person is quoted. S1–S6 form the class set; you do not need to read all of them alone.
S1  Lives before persecution
Europe before 1933; Amsterdam in the 1930s
Jewish people had families, jobs, beliefs, interests and hopes. Some followed religious traditions; others did not. They spoke many languages and lived in many countries. Jewish life was diverse and continues today. Anne Frank was born in Frankfurt in 1929. Her family moved to Amsterdam in the 1930s. There she learned Dutch, made friends and went to a local school. Her life was more than what later happened to her.
Anne is one person, not a picture of every Jewish life. Antisemitism already existed before Nazi rule.
Think: Name one part of a person’s life beyond persecution.
Research basis: H1, H2.
S2  Exclusion from state jobs
7 April 1933 | Germany
A Nazi law began to remove Jewish people from state jobs. At first, there were some exceptions. The policy treated people unfairly because they were Jewish. It could take away their work and income. Officials who wrote and carried out such rules helped make exclusion happen.
This was a choice made and enforced by people. It was not the fault of those targeted.
Think: What could losing a job change in a person’s life?
Research basis: H3.

Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 2 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W02
White paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
S3  Citizenship rights taken away
15 September 1935 and later rules | Germany
The Nuremberg Laws, followed by more rules, took away German Jews’ citizenship rights. Jewish people lost political rights. Nazi rules used family ancestry to decide whom to target. The Nazi idea that Jews were a separate biological race was false. Jewish identity includes faith, culture, heritage and community.
A law can be unjust. A state’s rule does not make persecution right.
Think: What is the difference between a law and a fair law?
Research basis: H3, H4.
S4  Excluded from public schools
November 1938 | Germany
Jewish pupils were barred from public schools. Access to education was cut back. This also broke links with classmates and teachers. Earlier restrictions had already harmed Jewish life. These cards show some steps in Germany, not every step across Europe. Dates and rules differed in other countries.
State decisions and the people enforcing them removed rights over time. Events were not inevitable.
Think: Name a right affected and one effect on daily life.
Research basis: H3.

Tuesday 12 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 2 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W02
White paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
S5  Actions and inaction
Nazi rule, 1933–1945 | Germany and occupied Europe
Perpetrators planned or carried out persecution. For example, officials enforced rules that excluded Jewish people. Some witnesses did not help people who faced persecution. Historians may call them bystanders. Others gained from exclusion, for example by taking over jobs. Such actions could make them more involved in the harm.
People had different power, knowledge and risks. Roles could change. A short card cannot tell us every person’s reason. Responsibility was not equal.
Think: What did a person do or fail to do? What could that change?
Research basis: H5.
S6  Help in Amsterdam
1942–1944 | German-occupied Netherlands
Miep Gies was one of several people who helped eight Jewish people hiding in Amsterdam. They included Anne Frank and her family. Miep brought food and library books. The people in hiding also made choices to protect their lives. Helping could bring serious danger. Only a small minority helped rescue Jewish people.
The eight were arrested in August 1944. Anne died in 1945. Help mattered, but it could not guarantee survival. We remember Anne’s life as well as her death.
Think: What help did Miep give? Why should we avoid a simple happy ending?
Research basis: H2, H6, H7.

White paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
Learning outcome: Study the Holocaust sensitively (Holocaust Memorial Day).
The Holocaust was the planned persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany, its allies and those who helped them. It took place from 1933 to 1945. The Nazis also persecuted and murdered millions of other people. Their experiences were not all the same.
When and where
What to know
Before persecution | S1
Jewish people had varied lives, interests, beliefs, families and hopes.
7 April 1933 | Germany | S2
A law began removing Jews from state jobs. Early exceptions existed.
15 September 1935 and later rules | Germany | S3
Nuremberg Laws took away citizenship and political rights.
November 1938 | Germany | S4
Jewish pupils were barred from public schools.
1942–1944 | Amsterdam | S6
Miep Gies and other helpers supported people in hiding.
Be precise and respectful
Perpetrators caused harm. Bystanders did not directly act, but their choices varied. Rescuers helped, often at risk. Roles could change; responsibility was not equal.
Holocaust Memorial Day is 27 January. We learn on 12 January. We remember people’s lives and consider our responsibility to treat people with dignity.

Word help for careful history
Tuesday 12 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 2 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W02
White paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
Word
Meaning
Holocaust
Nazi Germany and its helpers persecuted and murdered six million European Jews.
antisemitism
Prejudice, hostility or hate directed at Jewish people.
rights
Freedoms and protections that people should have.
persecution
Unfair and harmful treatment aimed at a group of people.
citizenship
Legal membership of a state, linked to rights.
perpetrator
A person who plans or carries out a harmful act.
bystander
A witness who does not directly act. This label can hide different choices.
rescuer
A person who helps others escape persecution or survive it.
remembrance
Taking time to learn about and remember people who were harmed.
source summary
A short account based on checked evidence. These cards are summaries, not original records.
Say or point to a word for private help. No reading aloud is required.
Keep claims factual. A source summary can help us learn, but it cannot tell us every person’s thoughts.

Pink paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
These are teacher-written factual summaries. They are not archive extracts or testimony. No real person is quoted. S1–S6 form the class set; you do not need to read all of them alone.
S1  Lives before persecution
Europe before 1933; Amsterdam in the 1930s
Jewish people had families, jobs, beliefs, interests and hopes. Some followed religious traditions; others did not. They spoke many languages and lived in many countries. Jewish life was diverse and continues today. Anne Frank was born in Frankfurt in 1929. Her family moved to Amsterdam in the 1930s. There she learned Dutch, made friends and went to a local school. Her life was more than what later happened to her.
Anne is one person, not a picture of every Jewish life. Antisemitism already existed before Nazi rule.
Think: Name one part of a person’s life beyond persecution.
Research basis: H1, H2.
S2  Exclusion from state jobs
7 April 1933 | Germany
A Nazi law began to remove Jewish people from state jobs. At first, there were some exceptions. The policy treated people unfairly because they were Jewish. It could take away their work and income. Officials who wrote and carried out such rules helped make exclusion happen.
This was a choice made and enforced by people. It was not the fault of those targeted.
Think: What could losing a job change in a person’s life?
Research basis: H3.
Lives, rights and choices: cards
Tuesday 12 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 2 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W02
Pink paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
S3  Citizenship rights taken away
15 September 1935 and later rules | Germany
The Nuremberg Laws, followed by more rules, took away German Jews’ citizenship rights. Jewish people lost political rights. Nazi rules used family ancestry to decide whom to target. The Nazi idea that Jews were a separate biological race was false. Jewish identity includes faith, culture, heritage and community.
A law can be unjust. A state’s rule does not make persecution right.
Think: What is the difference between a law and a fair law?
Research basis: H3, H4.
S4  Excluded from public schools
November 1938 | Germany
Jewish pupils were barred from public schools. Access to education was cut back. This also broke links with classmates and teachers. Earlier restrictions had already harmed Jewish life. These cards show some steps in Germany, not every step across Europe. Dates and rules differed in other countries.
State decisions and the people enforcing them removed rights over time. Events were not inevitable.
Think: Name a right affected and one effect on daily life.
Research basis: H3.

Tuesday 12 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 2 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W02
Pink paper version. Read quietly, point, write, type, speak privately or direct a scribe. You may pass. No public answer or reading aloud is required.
S5  Actions and inaction
Nazi rule, 1933–1945 | Germany and occupied Europe
Perpetrators planned or carried out persecution. For example, officials enforced rules that excluded Jewish people. Some witnesses did not help people who faced persecution. Historians may call them bystanders. Others gained from exclusion, for example by taking over jobs. Such actions could make them more involved in the harm.
People had different power, knowledge and risks. Roles could change. A short card cannot tell us every person’s reason. Responsibility was not equal.
Think: What did a person do or fail to do? What could that change?
Research basis: H5.
S6  Help in Amsterdam
1942–1944 | German-occupied Netherlands
Miep Gies was one of several people who helped eight Jewish people hiding in Amsterdam. They included Anne Frank and her family. Miep brought food and library books. The people in hiding also made choices to protect their lives. Helping could bring serious danger. Only a small minority helped rescue Jewish people.
The eight were arrested in August 1944. Anne died in 1945. Help mattered, but it could not guarantee survival. We remember Anne’s life as well as her death.
Think: What help did Miep give? Why should we avoid a simple happy ending?
Research basis: H2, H6, H7.

Word
Meaning
Holocaust
Nazi Germany and its helpers persecuted and murdered six million European Jews.
antisemitism
Prejudice, hostility or hate directed at Jewish people.
rights
Freedoms and protections that people should have.
persecution
Unfair and harmful treatment aimed at a group of people.
citizenship
Legal membership of a state, linked to rights.
perpetrator
A person who plans or carries out a harmful act.
bystander
A witness who does not directly act. This label can hide different choices.
rescuer
A person who helps others escape persecution or survive it.
remembrance
Taking time to learn about and remember people who were harmed.
source summary
A short account based on checked evidence. These cards are summaries, not original records.
Say or point to a word for private help. No reading aloud is required.
Keep claims factual. A source summary can help us learn, but it cannot tell us every person’s thoughts.

Staff answers: accurate history
Tuesday 12 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 2 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W02
Definition and lives
The Holocaust was the planned persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany, its allies and those who helped them. It took place from 1933 to 1945. The Nazis also persecuted and murdered millions of other people. Their experiences were not all the same.
The focus is Jewish lives, exclusion and human decisions. Do not reduce Jewish identity to victimhood or to a false racial category. Jewish people had varied religious and secular lives. S1 uses Anne’s school and friends as one example, not a representative life for all Jews. Antisemitism predated 1933; do not present earlier Europe as free from prejudice.
Rights: date, place and nuance
S2: 7 April 1933, Germany. The civil-service law began excluding Jews from state employment. There were initial exemptions; do not say every Jewish person lost every job that day. A reasonable effect is loss of income or status.
S3: 15 September 1935, Germany. The Nuremberg Laws introduced citizenship restrictions; implementing rules in November defined who was targeted and stripped Jews of political rights. The pupil card therefore says the laws and later rules. Nazi racial classifications were false ideology, not science.
S4: November 1938, Germany. Jews were excluded from public schools and universities. The card focuses on pupils: lost access to education and separation from classmates. Do not imply all learning or every Jewish school ceased.
The sequence is selected, not complete. It is not a straight, inevitable path or a single Europe-wide timetable. Nazi Germany invaded the Netherlands in May 1940; later restrictions there affected Anne. Do not apply the German 1933/1935/1938 dates to Amsterdam.
Teacher-written model
This illustrative model is attributed to no real person. It is not testimony.
S2 dates the state-job law to 7 April 1933 in Germany. It began removing Jewish people from state work, though early exceptions existed. Losing work could remove income. Officials who enforced the rule helped persecution happen. Jewish people were not to blame.
Staff answers: actions and assessment
Tuesday 12 January 2027 | P2 | 40 minutes | Year A
Humanities | LAUNCH | Spring 1 Week 2 | HUM-LAUNCH-S1-W02
Roles with care
S5: perpetrators included people who planned or enforced persecution. A witness who did not help may be described as a bystander, but the label covers varied actions and can conceal involvement. Taking a job from which Jews were excluded could deepen a person’s stake in persecution. Do not equate every witness with every perpetrator or presume motives.
S6: Miep Gies was one helper among several. She brought food and books to eight people hiding in Amsterdam during 1942–1944. The eight were arrested in August 1944; Anne died in 1945. This is enough context. No death details are needed. Rescue was uncommon, carried risks and did not guarantee survival. People who were targeted also acted to protect their lives.
Accept: enforcing a school ban → denied education; witnessing exclusion without help → a person was left without that support; bringing food → helped sustain people in hiding. Distinguish what evidence says from a plausible effect. Never ask what pupils would have done in those circumstances.
Hinge and follow-up
Which explains a change to rights? A: 1938 came after 1935. B: The school ban cut access to education and separated pupils from classmates. C: Every country used the same rules on the same date.
B. A orders dates but gives no effect. C is false: place and date matter. Check both learners privately. If either needs help, model S2 as date + change + effect, then use the parallel check before independent work.
Parallel check: What did the 1935 laws and later rules take away from German Jews? Answer: citizenship and political rights. Ask the learner to identify Germany and explain that law does not mean fairness.
Judge the common finish
Keep your own record: one fact about Jewish life before persecution; two dated changes to rights with source codes and an effect; one action or inaction for each of the three roles; and one thought on remembrance and care today.
A short table or exact directed pointing can meet the same core demand. Supported: frames and private reading. Independent: chosen evidence and effects. Aspire: a reasoned limit of labels or rescue. Do not reward length or guess independent reading from adult-read work.
Closing examples: remember the full lives of those harmed; check historical claims with a trusted source; report antisemitic abuse safely to a trusted adult; treat people with dignity. Do not equate an everyday disagreement with the Holocaust or promise that a single kind act prevents genocide.
Offer to the Communication portfolio. Record R only after the learner gives an idea, an adult audience replies with one NS (next step), and the learner responds in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. Record E only after actual banking. Keep the response mode and help used. A partner answer does not establish both learners’ understanding.

shapes.text: Rejoin with a private recap or a neutral daily-times task.

slides.notes:
Point to PAUSE or tell the adult quietly. Use the agreed supervised place. You do not need to explain to the group. When ready, choose a private recap or the quiet task. The adult will help you rejoin.
Agree a discreet PAUSE signal, named responsible adult within the school’s usual arrangements, supervised quiet place and return check before starting. If supervision away from the room is unavailable, offer a calm space in the room and seek normal support. If the sole adult cannot supervise both learners, pause the whole group. Do not send a pupil away alone.
Quiet task: put these times in order: 14:00 club; 08:30 library; 12:00 lunch; 10:00 break. Copy or point to the first and last. Add a clock face if you wish. These are made-up daily times. You do not need to use the history cards.
Record deferred history honestly; the quiet task is not evidence of the history outcome.

slides.title: Lives before persecution

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: Jewish people had varied families, beliefs, jobs and hopes.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: S1: Anne Frank made friends and went to school in Amsterdam.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Name one part of a person’s life beyond persecution.

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: One life does not stand for all Jewish lives. Jewish life continues today.

slides.notes: Use S1. Jewish people had diverse religious and secular lives, languages, occupations and hopes. Anne is one named example. The family moved to Amsterdam in the 1930s; this is before the German occupation of the Netherlands in May 1940. Do not apply German restriction dates to Amsterdam. Antisemitism existed before 1933. No pupil must disclose a personal connection.

slides.title: The Holocaust and our focus

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: Nazi Germany and its helpers persecuted and murdered six million European Jews (1933–1945).

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: We study lives, changes to rights and choices made by people.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Use dates and sources. Link actions to effects. Treat people with dignity.

shapes.name: distinction
shapes.text: Other groups also faced Nazi persecution and murder. Their experiences differed.

slides.notes:
The Holocaust was the planned persecution and murder of six million European Jews by Nazi Germany, its allies and those who helped them. It took place from 1933 to 1945. The Nazis also persecuted and murdered millions of other people. Their experiences were not all the same.
Success: life beyond victimhood; two dated restrictions and effects; actions of perpetrators, bystanders and rescuers; remembrance and responsibility today. Define persecution and antisemitism with the word mat. Jewish identity is not a biological race. Nazi racial claims were false.

slides.title: Link a change to its effect

shapes.name: stage-title
shapes.text: Link a change to its effect

shapes.name: model-label
shapes.text: Teacher-written model. No historical person is quoted.

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: S2: 7 April 1933, Germany. A law began removing Jews from state jobs.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: Early exceptions existed. Losing work could take away income.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Officials enforced the rule. A state’s law can be unjust.

slides.notes:
S2 dates the state-job law to 7 April 1933 in Germany. It began removing Jewish people from state work, though early exceptions existed. Losing work could remove income. Officials who enforced the rule helped persecution happen. Jewish people were not to blame.
Model date + place + change + effect. State the early exceptions to the state-job law. Explaining choices does not excuse them. Ask each learner privately for an effect through their chosen response mode.

slides.title: Rights were removed in steps

shapes.name: table-question
shapes.text: Choose a change. Explain its effect. Was the law fair?

tables: Work and income put at risk
slides.notes:
Use S2–S4. The 1935 date is the laws’ enactment; implementing rules in November removed political rights and defined Nazi categories. These were racist classifications, not scientific truths. November 1938 exclusion is from public schools, not a claim that every form of Jewish learning ended. Escalation was not inevitable.
Which explains a change to rights? A: 1938 came after 1935. B: The school ban cut access to education and separated pupils from classmates. C: Every country used the same rules on the same date.
B. A orders dates but gives no effect. C is false: place and date matter. Check both learners privately. If either needs help, model S2 as date + change + effect, then use the parallel check before independent work.
Parallel check: What did the 1935 laws and later rules take away from German Jews? Answer: citizenship and political rights. Ask the learner to identify Germany and explain that law does not mean fairness.

slides.title: Look at actions and effects

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: S5: Perpetrators planned or carried out persecution.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: S5: Some bystanders saw exclusion and did not help.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: S6: Miep Gies brought food and books to people in hiding.

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: Find an action, then explain its effect. Swap learning roles. Keep your own ideas.

slides.notes: Learning roles: Evidence Finder locates the card and action; Explainer links it to an effect. Swap after one example. Use all three historical roles; no pupil acts as a historical person. Perpetrators included officials enforcing exclusion. Some witnesses did not help; actions, power, knowledge and risks varied, and responsibility was not equal. People could move between roles. Miep was one of several helpers, not a lone rescuer. The people in hiding also acted to protect their lives. Rescue was uncommon and did not guarantee survival: the eight were arrested in August 1944 and Anne died in 1945. No further death details are needed. Do not guess motives or ask what pupils would have done.

slides.title: Your own record

shapes.name: task-main
shapes.text: Keep a fact about Jewish life, two dated rights changes, three role examples and a remembrance thought.

shapes.name: route-body-0
shapes.text: Use S1, S2 and S4, then S5–S6. Choose a frame and private reading if useful.

shapes.name: route-body-1
shapes.text: Choose two changes from S2–S4. Use dates, place and sources. Explain actions with S5–S6.

shapes.name: route-body-2
shapes.text: Keep the core record. Add a limit of role labels or rescue. Do not guess motives.

slides.notes:
Keep your own record: one fact about Jewish life before persecution; two dated changes to rights with source codes and an effect; one action or inaction for each of the three roles; and one thought on remembrance and care today.
Give just one task route. Supported retains the same core demand, with private reading, pointing, choices and exact scribing. Independent chooses two restrictions. Aspire adds one limit of labels or rescue. The individual evidence sheet provides a small table. Fade the model; record the help actually used. A partner’s response is not both pupils’ work.

slides.title: Check facts and effects

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: Have you kept a fact about life before persecution?

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: Do both rights changes have a date, place, source and effect?

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Have you linked each role to an action or inaction?

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: Read or hear one next step. Make your own response.

slides.notes:
Offer to the Communication portfolio. Record R only after the learner gives an idea, an adult audience replies with one NS (next step), and the learner responds in the same colour, on the same page or usual mode. Record E only after actual banking. Keep the response mode and help used. A partner answer does not establish both learners’ understanding.
Check the place and date, and the difference between a supported inference about an effect and a known fact. If work is incomplete or deferred, record that instead of inferring success.

slides.title: Remembrance and responsibility

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: One way to act with care today is ____.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Check facts. Treat people with dignity. Seek safe adult help for abuse.

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: You may respond privately or pass. Holocaust Memorial Day is 27 January.

slides.notes: Offer a private or written reflection, with passing allowed. Examples: remembering full lives; checking historical claims; treating people with dignity; reporting antisemitic abuse safely to a trusted adult. Do not equate everyday disagreements with the Holocaust or claim that one kind action prevents genocide. Holocaust Memorial Day is 27 January. Check readiness to leave and use normal pastoral follow-up if needed.

slides.title: Words for careful history

shapes.name: def-0
shapes.text: Prejudice, hostility or hate directed at Jewish people.

shapes.name: def-1
shapes.text: Unfair and harmful treatment aimed at a group.

shapes.name: def-2
shapes.text: A person who plans or carries out a harmful act.

shapes.name: def-3
shapes.text: A witness who does not directly act. Choices vary.

shapes.name: def-4
shapes.text: A person who helps others escape persecution or survive.

slides.notes: Available throughout, no additional time. Read a term privately on request. Add rights, citizenship and remembrance from the printed word mat. A bystander label can conceal involvement; examine actions rather than fixed labels. Do not debate the validity of antisemitic claims.

slides.title: Care and calm staff responses

shapes.name: body-0
shapes.text: Agree a discreet signal, supervised pause place and private return.

shapes.name: body-1
shapes.text: Stop antisemitism firmly. Correct facts calmly. Do not debate denial.

shapes.name: body-2
shapes.text: Reset respect after flippancy. Follow up privately and check those affected.

shapes.name: body-3
shapes.text: No graphic material, camp photos, testimony, disclosure or historical role play.

shapes.name: body-4
shapes.text: Quiet task ≠ history outcome. Record actual help, responses and deferred work.

slides.notes:
Before teaching, review the school’s chosen memorial-day resource with the designated lead. Use it as a staff reference and check it against these care rules. No extra footage, camp photographs, testimony, graphic imagery or unplanned live browsing is used in this lesson.
Preview the content privately where helpful. Do not ask pupils to imagine being victims, take historical roles, defend prejudice, rank suffering or disclose family history. Never appoint a Jewish pupil as a spokesperson. The sources are original factual summaries, not testimony or archive extracts.
Agree a discreet PAUSE signal, named responsible adult within the school’s usual arrangements, supervised quiet place and return check before starting. If supervision away from the room is unavailable, offer a calm space in the room and seek normal support. If the sole adult cannot supervise both learners, pause the whole group. Do not send a pupil away alone.
For distress, stop the demand, acknowledge it calmly and offer the agreed route without a public explanation or sanction. Do not probe or insist on a historical recap while the pupil is upset. Listen to disclosures and follow the school’s existing safeguarding arrangements; record only what is needed in the appropriate private system.
For an antisemitic remark, interrupt calmly and firmly. Name the harm without repeating a slur. Explain that hostility towards Jewish people is antisemitism and is unacceptable. Jewish people were not responsible for their persecution. Correct the falsehood with a brief fact; do not debate Holocaust denial or ask pupils to defend Jewish people’s rights.
For flippancy or laughter, stop and reset the expectation of respect. A nervous response is possible, but harm still needs addressing. Follow up privately, check those affected and use existing behaviour and safeguarding procedures for targeted, repeated or serious incidents. Avoid public shaming or speculative labels about the pupil.
Offer the neutral quiet task and a private check on readiness to return. The alternative is not evidence of the Holocaust outcome. Record the history work as deferred or not yet evidenced, with a later supported offer. There is no penalty for taking the agreed pause.
Quiet task: put these times in order: 14:00 club; 08:30 library; 12:00 lunch; 10:00 break. Copy or point to the first and last. Add a clock face if you wish. These are made-up daily times. You do not need to use the history cards.
Research: United States Holocaust Memorial Museum and Anne Frank House; titles and scopes are in SOURCE_MANIFEST.json. No web address or reproduced source text is supplied.
